sections.label: Constitution equality before law
sections.summary: Article 12 of the Constitution provides that all persons are equal before the law and entitled to equal protection of the law.

sentences.speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
sentences.text: Our Constitution provides at Article 12 that all persons are equal before the law and entitled to the equal protection of the law.

sections.label: English literacy survey findings
sections.summary: The General Household Survey 2015 shows nearly 20% of the population above 15 years old are not literate in English.

sentences.speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
sentences.text: Indeed, according to the General Household Survey 2015, there remains nearly 20% of the population above 15 years old who are not literate in English.

sections.label: Court document translations proposal
sections.summary: The national language policy recognises Chinese, Malay and Tamil as official languages, and the question is whether courts could provide translations of court documents to litigants in these languages, free or for a nominal fee.

sentences.speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
sentences.text: As the national language policy recognises Chinese, Malay and Tamil as official languages, I wonder if the courts could consider providing translations of court issued documents to litigants in these languages, either for free or for a nominal fee.

sections.label: Support for litigants in person
sections.summary: A litigant in person suffered a stroke and is weaker, and the question is how litigants in person have been supported during COVID-19 and how urgent cases can be flagged for expedited handling.

sentences.speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
sentences.text: In the meantime, he suffered a stroke and is much weaker now.

sentences.speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
sentences.text: So, my final point is, how have litigants in person been supported during COVID-19, and how can urgent cases be flagged out for expedited handling?

sections.label: New Rules of Court language
sections.summary: The new Rules of Court, scheduled to come into operation later this year, will be written in modern, layman language that is easy to understand and apply.

sentences.speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
sentences.text: The new Rules of Court, which is scheduled to come into operation later this year, will be written in modern, layman language, easy to understand and to apply.

sections.label: Backlogged cases re-fixed for hearing
sections.summary: As of present-date, the vast majority of backlogged cases have been re-fixed for hearing and many have already been disposed of.

sentences.speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
sentences.text: Nonetheless, as of present-date, the vast majority of the cases which have been backlogged have been re-fixed for hearing and many have already been disposed of.

sections.label: Remote hearings and court video facilities
sections.summary: Remote hearings are convenient, but those unable to attend remotely may ask for physical hearings or use dedicated court video-conferencing facilities.

sentences.speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
sentences.text: Remote hearings serve to make it more convenient for the user, ultimately, but those who are unable to do so can ask for their matters to be heard physically if they are unable to attend remotely.

sentences.speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
sentences.text: Alternatively, the Courts have also set up dedicated video-conferencing facilities in the Courts to cater to litigants who themselves lack the means or knowledge to connect via video-conferencing facilities.

sections.label: Exclusion Orders for recalcitrant respondents
sections.summary: Exclusion Orders target the most egregious cases, with only two since October 2015, requiring repeated non-compliance over about 17 to 18 months.

sentences.speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
sentences.text: Such an order is intended to deal with the most egregious of cases.

sentences.speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
sentences.text: There have only been two Exclusion Orders since October 2015.

sentences.speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
sentences.text: The CDRT can only make an Exclusion Order if the respondent has failed to comply with the initial CDRT order as well as the subsequent Special Direction; two times.

sentences.speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
sentences.text: The timeline in both cases for the EO roughly have been about 17 to 18 months, between the initial CDRT order and the Exclusion Order.

sentences.speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
sentences.text: So, for a period of more than one year, almost one and half years, this individual defendant has been disregarding the initial order, have been heard by the Courts and yet chose not to comply with the initial court order.

sentences.speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
sentences.text: Hence, where the Court is shown evidence that the respondent is recalcitrant and continues to cause nuisance to his neighbour in contravention of the court order and remains in continuous default, it is only right that firm measures be taken to stop the offending conduct and deter the continuation of the nuisance.

sections.label: Translation and pro bono lawyer help
sections.summary: CDCs with LSPBS are looking into full translation of court documents, and pro bono lawyers can assist with translation, elucidation and explanation.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: As I outlined earlier, this is something that is being looked into by the CDCs working with LSPBS.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: In the appropriate cases, we can consider a full translation of the court document.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: But I think Ms Lim would also appreciate that it is not in every case that a full translation automatically means that the person who is receiving this document, even in its translated language, can readily understand it.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: That is why the suggestion earlier that I made, which I think Ms Hany Soh also weighed in on, is for pro bono lawyers to assist in this process, not just in the translation but also in the elucidation and explanation of the impact of the document and what it means to the litigant-in-person.
